channels.name: Nevada Bureau of Health Care Quality and Compliance (HCQC)
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses, certifies and investigates health care facilities in Nevada, including facilities for the treatment of alcohol and drug abuse and residential psychiatric facilities. Investigators use interviews, records reviews and in-person observation.
channels.who_to_report: An HCQC-licensed facility - complaints about patient care or about how the facility is run.
channels.how: Call the complaint intake line; a message can be left at any hour and calls are returned within 48 to 72 hours. A complaint form can also be faxed to 702-486-6520.
channels.phone_note: Complaint intake. Messages can be left 24/7; calls returned in 48 to 72 hours.
channels.note: You may give your name or stay anonymous, and if you give it you can ask that it be kept confidential during the investigation. Every complaint is triaged by how much harm it suggests: a serious one can start an investigation within 48 hours, a lesser one waits for staff to be free.

channels.name: Nevada child abuse and neglect reporting
channels.what_it_can_do: Starts a child protective services investigation. Which agency takes the report depends on the county.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a Nevada program. Report to the county the program is in: Clark County (Las Vegas and Henderson) on 702-399-0081, Washoe County (Reno and Sparks) on 833-900-7233, and the Division of Child and Family Services for every other county on 833-571-1041.
channels.how: Call the number for that county. In the rural counties, out of hours and at weekends, the Division tells you to call local law enforcement to make the report instead. In an emergency, 911.
channels.phone_note: Division of Child and Family Services, for counties other than Clark and Washoe.

channels.name: Nevada Disability Advocacy and Law Center
channels.what_it_can_do: Nevada's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A Nevada program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: There is no SOL for CSA, sex trafficking, and CSAM claims against perpetrators for all past and future offenses. The SOL for claims against other defendants is age 38 with revival up to age 38.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for sexual assault if a report is filed by age 36. If a report is not filed by age 36, the SOL for sexual assault is age 36, or age 43 if the abuse was not reasonably discoverable by age 36. For other CSA felonies, the SOL is age 36 with a discovery rule.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking is the same as the SOL for sexual assault.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM violations is 3 years from the offense.

states.note: New Hampshire has a Special Investigations Unit that exists to investigate allegations of abuse and neglect in institutional settings and residential facilities, rather than leaving them to an ordinary district office. It also has an Office of the Child Advocate whose remit expressly covers any organisation certified or contracted to provide direct services to children - which means the residential facilities themselves, not only the state agency.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Three years for all personal injury claims, including assault, battery, false imprisonment and negligence. If you could not reasonably have discovered the injury and its cause at the time, the three years run from when you did or should have.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Yes. Someone hurt as a child may sue within two years after turning 18 (so by age 20), or within the normal three years from the injury if that is later. The general discovery rule in 508:4 also applies. No special extended period for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: State of New Hampshire: sue within three years of the injury and give written notice to the agency within 180 days (late notice does not bar the claim unless the state shows it was substantially prejudiced). Towns, cities and counties: three years, with notice to the clerk by registered mail within 60 days.
items.citation: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. 541-B:14, IV (state); 507-B:7 (governmental units)

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Six years from the offense for felony physical abuse of a child (charged as second-degree assault, which includes knowingly injuring a child under 13). Endangering the welfare of a child is usually a misdemeanor: one year. The clock does not pause until 18 for physical abuse; the 22-years-after-18 rule is for sexual offenses and incest only.
items.citation: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. 625:8, I(a)-(c); offenses 631:2, I(d) and 639:3

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Six years from the offense for felony assault (first- or second-degree assault). Misdemeanor (simple) assault: one year.
items.citation: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. 625:8, I; assault offenses 631:1, 631:2, 631:2-a

channels.name: New Hampshire Board of Mental Health Practice
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and regulates New Hampshire's mental health professionals and disciplines them. It treats a communication about alleged misconduct as a complaint where, if true, the conduct could breach the ethical codes, the administrative rules or the law. It publishes its board actions.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed mental health professional in New Hampshire. Psychologists have their own board under the same Office of Professional Licensure and Certification.
channels.how: File through the Board's complaints page.
channels.note: New Hampshire's online licence verification shows a licensee's current status and its disciplinary documents, so you can check what has already been found against them.

channels.name: New Hampshire Board of Psychologists
channels.what_it_can_do: Regulates and licenses the psychology profession in New Hampshire and disciplines its licensees.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed psychologist.
channels.how: File through the Office of Professional Licensure and Certification.

channels.name: New Hampshire DCYF child abuse and neglect hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The statewide report line, staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays. Allegations arising in foster homes, institutional settings and residential facilities go to a Special Investigations Unit rather than to a district office.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New Hampshire program. Residential child care facilities are themselves required to report suspected abuse to this number.
channels.how: Call.
channels.phone_note: 24 hours a day, including weekends and holidays.

channels.name: New Hampshire DHHS residential child care licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses New Hampshire's residential child care facilities under the He-C 4001 rules and enforces them, including the requirement that facilities report suspected abuse themselves.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed residential child care facility.
channels.how: Contact DHHS through its DCYF contact directory.
channels.phone_note: The DCYF line is the reporting route facilities themselves are required to use.

channels.name: New Hampshire Office of the Child Advocate
channels.what_it_can_do: An independent office reviewing complaints about children currently or previously involved with the state's child-serving agencies, and expressly about any organisation certified or contracted to provide direct services to children and families - residential facilities included.
channels.who_to_report: A young person who has been through a New Hampshire residential facility or the state system, whether or not they are still in it.
channels.how: Contact the office directly.

channels.name: Disability Rights Center - New Hampshire
channels.what_it_can_do: New Hampshire's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A New Hampshire program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: There is no SOL for incest and sexual assault of minors against any defendants and there is a permanent revival window for expired claims. The remaining claims have an SOL of age 30.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking claims is age 28 or 10 years after release from the trafficking situation, whichever is later.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM claims is age 20.
criminal: CSA: The SOL is age 40 for sexual assault and incest, age 24 for other felonies, and age 19 for misdemeanors.
Trafficking: The SOL is age 38 for trafficking offenses.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM violations is 6 years from the offense.

states.note: Two things New Jersey states plainly. Every report of abuse or neglect in an institutional setting - and it names residential treatment centres specifically - must go to the State Central Registry, and an investigator has to start within 24 hours. And a complaint form sent to a professional board is a government record: the board may be obliged to hand it to anyone who asks for it once the investigation is over.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Two years for personal injury, which covers assault, battery and negligence alike.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Yes. If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the two years do not start until you turn 18, so the deadline is usually your 20th birthday. There is no general extended deadline for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Against the state, a county, a town or another public entity, you must file a notice of claim within 90 days (a judge may allow late notice up to one year for extraordinary circumstances) and sue within two years; a minor can do both after turning 18.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: For endangering the welfare of a child (which includes a caregiver causing a child physical abuse or neglect): five years after the victim turns 18, or two years after the victim discovers the offense, whichever is later. Other child cruelty charges (a fourth-degree crime) have the general five years from the offense.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Five years from the offense for aggravated assault and other indictable crimes. Simple assault (a disorderly persons offense): one year.

channels.name: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, professional boards
channels.what_it_can_do: Houses the Professional Counselor Examiners Committee, the Board of Social Work Examiners, the State Board of Psychological Examiners and the State Board of Marriage and Family Therapy Examiners, and takes complaints against all of them through one portal.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor, social worker, psychologist or marriage and family therapist in New Jersey.
channels.how: File through the Division's board complaint portal, or post the board's form to its Newark address.
channels.mail: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, 124 Halsey Street, Newark, NJ 07101
channels.note: The Division warns that anything you put on the complaint form may become public. The completed form is a government record, and once any investigation is finished the board may be obliged to release it to anyone who requests it.

channels.name: New Jersey State Central Registry (1-877 NJ ABUSE)
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line for child abuse and neglect. New Jersey requires every report of abuse in an institutional setting - child care centres, schools, foster homes and residential treatment centres - to come here, and the Division of Child Protection and Permanency must start investigating within 24 hours.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New Jersey program. You do not need proof, and you can report anonymously.
channels.how: Call the 24-hour line. If the child is in immediate danger, call 911 as well.
channels.phone_note: 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights New Jersey
channels.what_it_can_do: New Jersey's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. It publishes its own guide to reporting abuse or neglect in New Jersey.
channels.who_to_report: A New Jersey program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line, or start from its reporting guide.

channels.name: New Jersey DCF Office of Licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Children and Families' licensing and regulatory authority for youth and residential programs, children's group homes, resource family homes and adoption agencies. It inspects them and investigates health and safety violations.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed New Jersey youth or residential program. Allegations of abuse go to the State Central Registry instead.
channels.how: Call the licensing complaint line or file online. Complaints may be made anonymously.
channels.note: Inspection and violation reports, and a summary of any complaint made against a licensed centre, have to be made available on request.

civil: The civil SOL for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM claims against all defendants is age 55 or 7 years after discovering an injury caused by the abuse, even for claims that have already expired.
criminal: CSA: There is no SOL for felony or aggravated sexual assault. The SOL for criminal sexual conduct and endangering the welfare of a child is age 23. The SOL for other felonies is 5 years from the offense, and 1 year for misdemeanors, with discovery and DNA rules.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking offenses is 5 years from the offense.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM offenses is age 23 or 2 years from the victim’s discovery of the offense, whichever is later.

states.note: New Mexico deserves a warning its own government has already published. The state Department of Justice reported that CYFD, which licenses congregate care and behavioral health settings, had no written policies or procedures governing how its Licensing and Certification Authority investigates allegations of abuse or neglect in those facilities, and recommended it adopt and publish some. Report anyway - but pair it with the Protection and Advocacy agency and with Statewide Central Intake rather than relying on the licensor alone.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Three years for an injury to the person, which covers assault, battery, false imprisonment and negligence.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Yes, but short. A minor has until one year after turning 18 (age 19), or three years from the injury, whichever gives more time. No general extended deadline for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Against the state or a local public body (including state juvenile facilities): written notice within 90 days of the incident (unless the government had actual notice) and suit within two years. Minority does not extend the two years, except that a child under 7 has until the 9th birthday.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: The clock for child abuse does not start until the child turns 18 or the abuse is reported to law enforcement, whichever comes first. Then five years for a third-degree felony (most first offenses without great bodily harm) or six years for a second-degree felony; abuse causing great bodily harm is a first-degree felony and may have no limit.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Five years from the offense for felony aggravated battery (a third-degree felony); six years for a second-degree felony. Misdemeanor battery: two years (petty misdemeanor simple battery: one year).

channels.name: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, behavioral health boards
channels.what_it_can_do: Houses the Counseling and Therapy Practice Board, the Social Work Board and the Psychologist Examiners Board, takes complaints against their licensees and runs the disciplinary proceedings against those who break the practice laws.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor, therapist, social worker or psychologist in New Mexico. All three boards share a phone number and a mailing address.
channels.how: Use the Department's boards complaint form.
channels.mail: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, PO Box 25101, Santa Fe, NM 87504

channels.name: New Mexico CYFD, Licensing and Certification Authority
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses congregate care and behavioral health settings in New Mexico, monitors their programming, and is the body responsible for ensuring trauma-responsive care.
channels.what_it_cannot_do: The New Mexico Department of Justice found it had no written policies or procedures for how it investigates abuse and neglect allegations in the facilities it licenses, and no statewide tracking to stop somebody who has abused a child working at another licensed facility. Treat a report here as necessary but not sufficient.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed congregate care or behavioral health facility in New Mexico.
channels.how: Contact CYFD. Report the same facts to Statewide Central Intake and to Disability Rights New Mexico as well, and keep your own record of what you sent and when.

channels.name: New Mexico CYFD Statewide Central Intake
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line for child abuse and neglect, open around the clock.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New Mexico program.
channels.how: Call.
channels.phone_note: 1-855-333-SAFE. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights New Mexico
channels.what_it_can_do: New Mexico's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. Given what the state's own Department of Justice found about CYFD's investigations, this is a more important channel in New Mexico than in most states.
channels.who_to_report: A New Mexico program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for CSA claims against all defendants is age 24 with a 3-year discovery rule.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for trafficking claims is age 28.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM claims against all defendants is age 24 with a 3-year discovery rule.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for first-degree felonies, including CSA. The SOL is age 23 for non-first-degree abandonment or abuse, criminal sexual penetration, or criminal sexual contact. The SOL for other felonies is 5 or 6 years from commission, and 2 years for misdemeanors.
Trafficking: There is no SOL for trafficking of victims under age 13. The SOL is 6 years from the offense for trafficking victims under age 16.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM is 6 years from the offense for second-degree felony violations and 5 years from the offense for third- and fourth-degree felony violations.

states.note: New York has something most states do not: the Justice Center for the Protection of People with Special Needs, created by statute in 2013, with its own 24-hour register, its own investigators and the power to support criminal prosecution. It says every allegation is investigated to conclusion, and it provides advocates to victims and families during the investigation. If the program is a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility, this is the strongest channel in the state.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: One year for intentional harm: assault, battery and false imprisonment. Three years for negligence (for example, a program's negligent supervision or hiring). If the person who hurt you is criminally prosecuted, you get at least one year after the criminal case ends to sue them.
items.citation: N.Y. C.P.L.R. 215(3) (intentional torts, 1 year); 214(5) (personal injury/negligence, 3 years); 215(8)(a) (criminal-action extension)

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Yes. For a one-year claim (assault, battery), the time you were under 18 is not counted, so the deadline is your 19th birthday. For a three-year negligence claim, you have three years after turning 18 (your 21st birthday). The 10-year cap in this statute does not apply to minors except in medical malpractice. No general extended period for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Against a county, city, town, village or school district: serve a notice of claim within 90 days and sue within one year and 90 days. Against New York State (Court of Claims): file the claim, or a notice of intention to file, within 90 days; then the claim is due within two years for negligence or one year for intentional torts. Minors get extra time under the tolling rules.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Five years from the offense for felony physical abuse of a child (charged as felony assault). Endangering the welfare of a child is a misdemeanor: two years. The clock does not pause until the child is older for physical abuse; the age-23 rule applies only to sexual offenses, incest and child sexual performance.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Five years from the offense for felony assault (first- or second-degree). Misdemeanor (third-degree) assault: two years.

channels.name: New York Office of the Professions, Office of Professional Discipline
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates professional misconduct by anyone licensed by the State of New York - psychologists, mental health counselors, marriage and family therapists, creative arts therapists, psychoanalysts and social workers - and illegal practice by the unlicensed. Outcomes run from a warning letter to revoking the licence.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed mental health professional in New York, or someone practising without the licence.
channels.how: Complete the discipline complaint form and post it to the regional Office of Professional Discipline nearest where the incident happened, or fax it. Complaints must be in writing; they cannot be made by phone, though you can call for help with the form.
channels.phone_note: For information on filing. The complaint itself has to be in writing. Fax 212-951-6420.
channels.note: Investigators in the regional office may consult members of the State board for that profession before deciding.

channels.name: New York State Justice Center for the Protection of People with Special Needs
channels.what_it_can_do: Runs the Vulnerable Persons Central Register, a 24-hour hotline for abuse, neglect, financial misappropriation and any significant incident threatening the health, safety or welfare of someone in a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility. It investigates every allegation to conclusion, and works with prosecutors on criminal cases arising from them.
channels.who_to_report: A young person with special needs - which includes a mental health diagnosis - receiving services at a New York state-operated, licensed or certified facility or program.
channels.how: Call the Vulnerable Persons Central Register. If somebody is in immediate danger, call 911 first.
channels.phone_note: Vulnerable Persons Central Register, 24 hours a day. Advocates for victims and families on 1-800-624-4143.
channels.note: The Justice Center provides advocates who answer questions about the process and give case updates during an investigation - unusual, and worth using.

channels.name: New York Statewide Central Register of Child Abuse and Maltreatment
channels.what_it_can_do: The state's child abuse hotline, run by the Office of Children and Family Services. Takes reports from the general public and routes them to the local child protective service for investigation.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New York program. Neighbours, relatives and concerned citizens can all use the public line.
channels.how: Call the 24-hour toll-free line. If a child is in immediate danger, call 911 or the local police first.
channels.phone_note: 24 hours a day. TDD/TTY 1-800-638-5163, or have a Video Relay provider call the main number.

channels.name: Disability Rights New York
channels.what_it_can_do: New York's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A New York program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

channels.name: New York OCFS and OMH residential facility oversight
channels.what_it_can_do: The Office of Mental Health regulates residential treatment facilities for children and youth, and the OCFS Regional Office investigates child abuse and neglect allegations involving facilities OMH licenses or operates. Between them they hold the licence and investigate what happens inside it.
channels.who_to_report: A New York residential treatment facility - unsafe conditions, inadequate supervision, hygiene and health neglect, anything that is a standards failure rather than one person's conduct.
channels.how: Report through the OCFS portal or the Statewide Central Register. For a licensed facility the Justice Center's Vulnerable Persons Central Register is usually the stronger route.
channels.phone_note: Statewide Central Register line used for reports about facilities.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for CSA is age 55 for claims against all defendants. A 2-year revival window for expired claims of sexual abuse of children and adults that occurred in NYC is open until March 1, 2025.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for sex trafficking is age 33 with a 15-year discovery rule.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM is age 55 for claims against all defendants.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for first-degree CSA offenses. The SOL is either age 28, 33 or 43 for other felonies, and age 25 for misdemeanors.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking is 5 years from the offense.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM violations is either age 28 or 5 years from when the offense was reported to law enforcement, whichever is earlier.

states.note: North Carolina keeps a separate board for each profession, so you have to know which licence the person holds before you can complain about them; every board publishes a licence lookup and it is worth checking first. Child abuse reporting is the other oddity: there is no statewide hotline, and a report goes to the department of social services in the county the program sits in.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Three years. The same three-year limit covers assault, battery and false imprisonment (from the date it happened) and negligence or other personal injury (from when the harm became apparent, with an outside limit of 10 years after the last act).

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Yes. If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the normal time limit (three years for assault or injury) does not start until you turn 18, so the usual deadline is your 21st birthday. There is no general extended deadline for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Negligence claims against a North Carolina state agency (for example a state-run juvenile facility) must be filed with the Industrial Commission within three years under the State Tort Claims Act; there is no general statutory notice-of-claim step for counties and cities.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: No time limit for felony child abuse. North Carolina has no statute of limitations for any felony. Misdemeanor child abuse must be charged within 10 years.
items.citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15-1 (limits misdemeanors only); felony child abuse is N.C. Gen. Stat. 14-318.4

items.label: Assault
items.summary: No time limit for felony assault, because North Carolina has no statute of limitations for felonies. Misdemeanor assault must be charged within two years.

channels.name: North Carolina Psychology Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates complaints against licensed psychologists and against people practising psychology without a licence, and can discipline a licence. It can also open an investigation on its own initiative, which it says is most likely when the information is already public.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed psychologist, or somebody presenting themselves as one.
channels.how: The online complaint form is the quickest route. There is a PDF form as an alternative, with separate written instructions.
channels.phone_note: Tuesday and Thursday, 8am to 5pm. Second line 828-265-8611.
channels.mail: North Carolina Psychology Board, 895 State Farm Road, Suite 101, Boone, NC 28607
channels.note: The Board's current website is ncpsychologyboard.info. Its old .org domain still serves the complaint form but the rest of the site has moved.

channels.name: North Carolina Board of Licensed Clinical Mental Health Counselors
channels.what_it_can_do: Takes complaints against Licensed Clinical Mental Health Counselors, refers them to its Ethics Committee, and disciplines licences. It publishes its disciplinary actions.
channels.who_to_report: An LCMHC. This is the licence most therapists in North Carolina programs hold.
channels.how: Download the Board's complaint form, cite the specific parts of the Code of Ethics or the Practice Act you say were breached, and post it or email it to the complaints address.
channels.mail: NCBLCMHC, P.O. Box 77819, Greensboro, NC 27417
channels.note: The Board asks you to try to resolve it with the counselor first, following the American Counseling Association's guidance. That is their preference, not a requirement, and it is not always a safe thing to do.

channels.name: North Carolina Social Work Certification and Licensure Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates complaints against social workers it certifies or licenses, and allegations of unlicensed clinical social work practice. It can also start its own investigation where there is reasonable cause.
channels.what_it_cannot_do: It has no legal authority to keep your identity from the social worker you complained about. It also has no authority over the many social workers who practise lawfully in North Carolina without a licence, so check the lookup first.
channels.who_to_report: A certified or licensed social worker, or somebody doing clinical social work without the licence it requires.
channels.how: Download the complaint form and post it with your documentation. Online submission was still being built when this was checked.
channels.note: The Board's site is ncswboard.gov. The similarly named .org domain has lapsed and now serves gambling spam - do not use it.

channels.name: North Carolina Marriage and Family Therapy Licensure Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates licensed marriage and family therapists, and also people who use the LMFT or LMFTA title, or imply they hold it, without the licence. That second power matters in an industry where titles get used loosely.
channels.who_to_report: An LMFT or LMFTA, or anyone practising marriage and family therapy in North Carolina without being licensed in a discipline that allows it.
channels.how: Use the online complaint form. A printable form can be requested from the Board if you cannot complete it online.
channels.mail: North Carolina Marriage and Family Therapy Licensure Board, PO Box 10912, Raleigh, NC 27605

channels.name: North Carolina Medical Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines physicians, including psychiatrists and any doctor serving as a program's medical director.
channels.who_to_report: A doctor. Therapists and counselors go to their own boards above.

channels.name: NC Division of Health Service Regulation, Complaint Intake
channels.what_it_can_do: The complaint route into the division that licenses and inspects mental health, substance use and developmental disability facilities in North Carolina, including residential programs for minors. It conducts complaint investigations and its Mental Health Licensure and Certification Section can act on a facility's licence.
channels.who_to_report: The facility: conditions, staffing, restraint, how it is run. Its Health Care Personnel Investigations section separately handles allegations against individual staff in licensed facilities.
channels.how: Call the complaint hotline during its posted hours, or use the written complaint form.
channels.phone_note: Within North Carolina. From elsewhere, 919-855-4500. Open 9am-12pm and 1pm-4pm on weekdays, holidays excepted - a narrow window, so allow for it.
channels.mail: Complaint Intake, 2711 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699-2711
channels.note: North Carolina publishes the resulting survey and deficiency reports, so it is worth searching what has already been cited against a program before you call.

channels.name: Your county Department of Social Services (child abuse report)
channels.what_it_can_do: North Carolina law requires any person or institution who suspects a child under 18 is abused or neglected to report it to the county department of social services. The county DSS investigates and can involve law enforcement.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a North Carolina program right now.
channels.how: There is no single statewide hotline. Find the DSS for the county the program is in and call it. If the danger is immediate, call 911.

channels.name: NC Department of Justice, Medicaid Investigations Division
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates fraud by Medicaid providers and, separately, physical abuse of any patient in a Medicaid-funded facility, along with theft or commingling of patients' funds. It brings cases; it has recovered over a billion dollars and has settled fraud allegations against North Carolina treatment centers.
channels.who_to_report: A Medicaid-funded program where a young person was physically abused, or where money went missing.
channels.how: Report online - there are separate forms for provider fraud and for patient abuse - or call.

channels.name: Disability Rights North Carolina
channels.what_it_can_do: North Carolina's Protection and Advocacy agency. It monitors facilities where people with disabilities live and receive services, investigates abuse and neglect, and publishes public reports on what it finds.
channels.what_it_cannot_do: It says plainly that it is not a regulatory body: it cannot license, fine or close a facility. Pair it with a report to DHSR.
channels.who_to_report: A North Carolina program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact its intake line. It publishes its own guide to reporting abuse and neglect in facilities, which names each agency and what it does.

civil: The civil SOL for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM claims is age 28 against all defendants with a very narrow discovery rule.
criminal: There is no criminal SOL for any felonies, including for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM. There is an SOL of 10 years from the offense for misdemeanor sexual battery, indecent liberties between children, and child abuse, and other misdemeanors have an SOL of 2 years from the offense.

states.note: North Dakota's reporting line is not staffed around the clock: live agents answer between 8am and 5pm Central on weekdays, and outside that you can only leave a message. If a child is in immediate danger at a weekend, call law enforcement rather than waiting on a callback. North Dakota law does require institutional abuse reports to be made and received the same way as every other report, so a program is not a special case.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Two years for assault, battery or false imprisonment. Six years for negligence and other personal injury that is not an intentional tort.
items.citation: N.D. Cent. Code 28-01-18(1) (assault, battery, false imprisonment: 2 years); 28-01-16(5) (other injury to the person: 6 years)

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Partly. Time while you are under 18 does not count, but the extension can last no longer than one year after you turn 18. In practice the deadline is your 19th birthday or the normal deadline counted from the injury, whichever is later. No general extended deadline for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: For claims against the State of North Dakota, written notice must go to the Office of Management and Budget within 180 days after the injury is discovered (one year for a serious injury), and the suit must be filed within three years; claims against cities, counties and other political subdivisions must be filed within three years.
items.citation: N.D. Cent. Code 32-12.2-04(1) (notice), 28-01-22.1 (state, 3 years), 32-12.1-10 (political subdivisions, 3 years)

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Three years from the offense for felony child abuse. There is no pause until the child turns 18 for physical abuse; the child-victim extensions apply only to sexual offenses and trafficking.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Three years from the offense for aggravated assault and other felonies. Misdemeanor (simple) assault: two years.

channels.name: North Dakota Board of Counselor Examiners
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines professional counselors in North Dakota.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed professional counselor.
channels.how: The complaint process begins once the Board's formal complaint form is signed and returned to its office.

channels.name: North Dakota State Board of Psychologist Examiners
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines psychologists, registrants and psychology residents in North Dakota.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed psychologist, registrant or psychology resident.
channels.how: Complete and sign the Board's complaint form, setting out the nature of the allegation and the facts behind it. You may attach supporting documents.

channels.name: North Dakota Board of Social Work Examiners
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses social workers in North Dakota and ensures they comply with the laws and regulations governing the practice.
channels.what_it_cannot_do: It cannot take a complaint over the phone, and the form has to be signed.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed social worker.
channels.how: Send a written, signed complaint to the Board.

channels.name: North Dakota Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Line
channels.what_it_can_do: The statewide report line. North Dakota law requires reports of known or suspected institutional child abuse or neglect to be made and received in the same way as any other report.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a North Dakota program.
channels.how: Call. Live agents answer 8am to 5pm Central on weekdays; outside those hours you can leave a message. If a child is in immediate danger, contact law enforcement.
channels.phone_note: Live 8am to 5pm Central, Monday to Friday. Messages can be left outside those hours.

channels.name: North Dakota HHS licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses North Dakota's child care and residential facilities and investigates complaints that one has breached the licensing standards.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed North Dakota facility.
channels.how: Contact Health and Human Services. Abuse and neglect go to the reporting line.
channels.phone_note: Child and Family Services; toll free 1-800-245-3736.

channels.name: North Dakota Protection and Advocacy Project
channels.what_it_can_do: North Dakota's federally mandated P&A, with authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A North Dakota program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for CSA claims against all defendants is age 36 for minors abused under age 15, and 21 years after the abuse for minors abused at age 15-17.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for trafficking claims is age 28.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM claims is age 36 for minors abused under age 15, and 21 years after the abuse for minors abused at age 15-17.
criminal: CSA: The SOL is age 36 for victims under age 15. The SOL is 2 or 3 years from the offense for other felonies and misdemeanors, with a DNA rule.
Trafficking: The SOL is age 22 for human trafficking of victims under age 15, while the SOL is 7 years for trafficking of victims aged 15 and older.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM violations is 3 years from the offense.

states.note: Ohio has something rare and worth knowing about: a Youth and Family Ombudsmen Office that takes complaints directly from young people, with a separate form for youth and for families. Most state oversight assumes an adult is doing the reporting. Ohio's child abuse line is also a directory rather than a call centre - it connects you to the county office that will actually handle it.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: One year for assault, battery or false imprisonment. Two years for other bodily injury claims, such as negligence (for example, a program that failed to protect you).

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the clock does not start until you turn 18. So assault or battery claims are due by your 19th birthday, and negligence claims by your 20th.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Claims against the State of Ohio go to the Court of Claims within two years (or a shorter period if one applies, such as one year for assault); claims against a county, city or other local government must be filed within two years, paused while the victim is a minor.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Six years for a felony. For crimes that injured a child in a way that suggests abuse or neglect, the six years do not start until the victim turns 18 or until a children services agency or police officer is told about the abuse, whichever comes first.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Six years for felony assault. Misdemeanor assault must be charged within two years.

channels.name: Ohio Counselor, Social Worker and Marriage and Family Therapist Board
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines counselors, social workers and marriage and family therapists in Ohio, and investigates complaints including incompetent practice, breaking confidentiality, failure to tell clients the nature and extent of services, sexual harassment, discrimination, physical or verbal abuse and conflict of interest.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor, social worker or marriage and family therapist in Ohio. Psychologists have their own board.
channels.how: File through the Board's eLicense complaint portal, or download the form and fax it.

channels.name: Ohio State Board of Psychology
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines psychologists and school psychologists in Ohio, and publishes how its investigation process works alongside its complaint form.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed psychologist in Ohio.
channels.how: Use the Board's complaint page, which sets out the investigation process as well as the form.

channels.name: Ohio Department of Behavioral Health
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and certifies behavioral health providers in Ohio, including residential treatment, and takes complaints about the services they give.
channels.who_to_report: A certified or licensed behavioral health provider or residential program.
channels.how: Contact the Department.
channels.note: Formerly the Ohio Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services (OhioMHAS); the old mha.ohio.gov address now redirects here.

channels.name: Ohio child abuse and neglect reporting line
channels.what_it_can_do: An automated directory that connects you straight to the child welfare or law enforcement office in the relevant county, which is where the report is actually handled.
channels.who_to_report: A child at an Ohio program. Report to the county the program is in.
channels.how: Call. Reports can be anonymous.

channels.name: Ohio Youth and Family Ombudsmen Office
channels.what_it_can_do: An independent office for anyone concerned about the Ohio children services system. It takes complaints directly from young people, with a separate route for youth and for families.
channels.who_to_report: A young person in the Ohio system who wants to complain themselves, or a family who has hit a wall with an agency.
channels.how: Use the Youth complaint form or the Family complaint form on the office's site.

channels.name: Disability Rights Ohio
channels.what_it_can_do: Ohio's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: An Ohio program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil CSA SOL is age 30 against all defendants with a fraudulent concealment tolling rule. A 5-year window opened on October 12, 2023 for expired claims against the bankruptcy estate of the Boy Scouts of America.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for trafficking is age 19.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM is age 19.
criminal: CSA: The criminal SOL is age 43 for rape and sexual battery, age 38 for other felonies, and age 20 for misdemeanors, with a D NA rule.
Trafficking: The SOL is age 38 for trafficking offenses.
CSAM: The SOL is age 38 for CSAM offenses.

states.note: Oklahoma has an Office of Client Advocacy whose investigations unit exists specifically to investigate abuse, neglect, exploitation and caretaker misconduct involving children in congregate care settings. That is unusually close to this industry, and it is a separate route from the general child abuse hotline. Oklahoma also splits complaints about a residential facility: anything rising to abuse or neglect goes to Child Welfare Services, everything else is investigated by Child Care Services.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: One year for assault, battery or false imprisonment. Two years for other injury claims, such as negligence.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, you get at least until one year after your 18th birthday to sue.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: For claims against the state, a county, city or public school, a written notice of claim must be filed within one year of the injury, and the lawsuit must be filed within 180 days after the claim is denied.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Child abuse charges under Oklahoma's child abuse law, including physical abuse and neglect, can be filed until the victim's 45th birthday.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Three years for most assaults, felony or misdemeanor. Seven years if a deadly weapon was used in a felony.

channels.name: Oklahoma State Board of Behavioral Health Licensure
channels.what_it_can_do: Enforces the rules governing Licensed Professional Counselors, Licensed Marital and Family Therapists and Licensed Behavioral Practitioners, and disciplines their licences. It also takes complaints about people delivering counseling services with no licence at all.
channels.who_to_report: An LPC, LMFT or LBP in Oklahoma, a candidate for one of those licences, or somebody practising without one. Psychologists are licensed separately by the Oklahoma State Board of Examiners of Psychologists.
channels.how: Oklahoma calls this a Request for Inquiry rather than a complaint. Anyone may file one, and it has to be in writing.
channels.mail: State Board of Behavioral Health Licensure, 3815 N Santa Fe, Ste. 110, Oklahoma City, OK 73118

channels.name: Oklahoma Office of Client Advocacy, Investigations Unit
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates abuse, neglect, exploitation and caretaker misconduct involving children living in Office of Juvenile Affairs facilities, day treatment programs and other congregate care settings.
channels.who_to_report: A child in an Oklahoma congregate care setting - which is what most programs in this industry are.
channels.how: Report online at abuseisnotok.org, call the statewide hotline, or contact OCA intake directly.
channels.phone_note: OCA Intake. The 24-hour statewide hotline is 1-800-522-3511.

channels.name: Oklahoma Statewide Child Abuse and Neglect Hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory 24-hour report line. Where a complaint about a residential child care facility rises to abuse or neglect it is referred to Child Welfare Services to screen and investigate; other allegations go to Child Care Services.
channels.who_to_report: A child at an Oklahoma program.
channels.how: Call, or report online through abuseisnotok.org.
channels.phone_note: 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights Oklahoma
channels.what_it_can_do: Oklahoma's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: An Oklahoma program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.
channels.note: Operates as Disability Rights Oklahoma (DROK); the older Oklahoma Disability Law Center name and okdlc.org address still redirect here.

channels.name: Oklahoma Human Services, Child Care Services licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses residential child care facilities in Oklahoma and investigates the complaint allegations that do not rise to abuse or neglect - conditions, staffing, supervision, compliance with the licensing requirements.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed Oklahoma residential facility, where the issue is how the place is run. Anything amounting to abuse or neglect is referred instead to Child Welfare Services.
channels.how: Report through the statewide hotline or the online reporting site; Oklahoma routes the allegation to whichever of the two units should handle it.

civil: The civil SOL for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM claims is age 45 against perpetrators and age 20 against all other defendants.
criminal: CSA: The criminal SOL for CSA is age 45 with a DNA rule, and 3 years from the offense for other felonies and misdemeanors.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking is age 45.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM offenses is age 45.

states.note: Oregon's mental health licensing boards sit under one agency, the Mental Health Regulatory Agency, which investigates on its own initiative as well as on complaints - it names newspaper articles and broadcasts as a reason it will open a case, which is unusually explicit. Licensees in Oregon are themselves required to report a colleague they believe is in breach, which is worth knowing if you are a clinician who has seen something.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Two years for assault, battery, false imprisonment or other injury, including negligence. Abuse suffered as a child has a much longer deadline (see below).

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: For physical or serious emotional abuse by an adult while you were under 18, you can sue until you turn 40, or within five years after you realize the abuse caused your injury, whichever is later. For other injuries, being a minor pauses the clock only until one year after your 18th birthday, and never by more than five years.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: For claims against a state agency, county, city or other public body, a notice of claim is due within 180 days of the injury, and the lawsuit within two years. Youth in the custody of the Department of Human Services or the Oregon Youth Authority do not need to give the notice for claims against those agencies.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: First-degree criminal mistreatment of a child (a felony) and felony strangulation: six years, or if the victim was under 18, before the victim turns 30 or within 12 years of a report to police or child welfare, whichever comes first. Other felony physical abuse such as assault: three years.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Three years for felony assault. Misdemeanor assault must be charged within two years.

channels.name: Oregon Mental Health Regulatory Agency
channels.what_it_can_do: Runs compliance for the Board of Licensed Professional Counselors and Therapists (LPCs, LMFTs and registered associates) and the Board of Psychology. Its staff investigate licensees, registrants and people practising without a licence, and the boards discipline those found in breach.
channels.who_to_report: A counselor, marriage and family therapist or psychologist in Oregon, or somebody practising as one without a licence. Social workers have their own board.
channels.how: Use the online complaint form for the relevant board.
channels.mail: Board of Licensed Professional Counselors and Therapists, 3218 Pringle Rd SE #120, Salem, OR 97302-6312
channels.note: The Board will not confirm who complained, and says it makes every effort to protect a complainant who wants anonymity - but warns that your identity may become obvious through the investigation itself.

channels.name: Oregon Health Authority, Licensing and Certification (Residential and Outpatient Behavioral Health Programs)
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and certifies residential and outpatient behavioral health programs in Oregon and investigates complaints about them. Every complaint is assigned to a compliance specialist who follows it up with you and with the program.
channels.who_to_report: The program itself.
channels.how: Fill in the Licensing and Certification Complaint Intake Form in full, attach supporting documents, and send it by secure email or post. You can also phone a member of the unit.
channels.mail: Licensing & Certification, 500 Summer Street NE - E86, Salem, OR 97301
channels.note: The Division aims to resolve a complaint within 30 days and sends a resolution letter saying what it found and what happens next.

channels.name: Oregon Child Abuse Hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line for child abuse and neglect, open every hour of every day. A Child Welfare screener takes the report.
channels.who_to_report: A child at an Oregon program. The Health Authority's own licensing pages send you here when abuse is suspected, rather than to the licensing complaint route.
channels.how: Call. The screener will ask for the child's name, age and where they are. What you tell them is kept confidential.
channels.phone_note: 855-503-SAFE. 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

channels.name: Disability Rights Oregon
channels.what_it_can_do: Oregon's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: An Oregon program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for CSA claims against all defendants is age 40 with a 5-year discovery rule and revival up to age 40.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking claims is the later of age 28 or 10 years after the trafficking ends.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM claims against all defendants is age 40 with a 5-year discovery rule.
criminal: CSA: The criminal SOL is age 30 for many CSA felonies and age 22 for third-degree sexual abuse, with a DNA elimination rule. The SOL is 3 years from the offense for any remaining felonies and 2 years from the offense for misdemeanors.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking is 3 years from the offense.
CSAM: The SOL for creation or possession of CSAM is either age 30 or 12 years after a report to law enforcement, whichever is earlier. The SOL is 3 years from the offense for other CSAM felonies.

states.note: Pennsylvania routes every complaint about a licensed professional through one bureau, the Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs, whichever board holds the licence. Its ChildLine is one of the clearer state hotlines: it takes both formal abuse referrals and general child well-being concerns, so you do not have to be certain you are describing abuse before you call.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Two years for assault, battery, false imprisonment, or injury caused by negligence.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the clock does not start until you turn 18. You then get the same two years as anyone else, so the deadline is your 20th birthday.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Before suing a state agency, county, school district or other government unit, you must file a written notice within six months of the injury; the lawsuit itself generally has the normal two-year deadline. Courts can excuse a late notice for a reasonable excuse.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Most physical abuse crimes must be charged within two years, or five years for aggravated assault. But if the abuser was a person responsible for the child's welfare, the clock does not start until the child turns 18.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Five years for aggravated assault. Simple assault and most other offenses must be charged within two years.

channels.name: Pennsylvania Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs (BPOA)
channels.what_it_can_do: Receives and processes every complaint against a state-licensed professional in Pennsylvania, including those under the State Board of Social Workers, Marriage and Family Therapists and Professional Counselors, and the State Board of Psychology. The Department's Bureau of Enforcement and Investigation does the investigating, and the boards discipline the licence.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed social worker, marriage and family therapist, professional counselor or psychologist in Pennsylvania. Any member of the public can file.
channels.how: Use the Department of State's complaint form for a PA-licensed professional.
channels.mail: State Board of Social Workers, Marriage and Family Therapists and Professional Counselors, P.O. Box 2649, Harrisburg, PA 17105-2649

channels.name: Pennsylvania ChildLine
channels.what_it_can_do: The statewide child protective services referral line. Trained specialists take both suspected abuse referrals and general child well-being concerns, and decide what happens next with each one.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a Pennsylvania program. You do not have to be sure it is abuse - ChildLine explicitly takes general well-being concerns too.
channels.how: Call, at any hour. Mandated reporters have a separate electronic route; permissive reporters - anyone else - may report anonymously.
channels.phone_note: 24 hours a day, seven days a week. TDD 1-866-872-1677.
channels.note: Pennsylvania distinguishes mandated reporters, who must report and have their own portal, from permissive reporters, who are encouraged to and may do so anonymously.

channels.name: Disability Rights Pennsylvania
channels.what_it_can_do: Pennsylvania's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A Pennsylvania program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

channels.name: Pennsylvania DHS, Office of Children, Youth and Families residential licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses the private providers running residential and day treatment, secure care and transitional living settings for children in Pennsylvania, alongside county child welfare offices. It inspects them, and can impose a provisional licence or revoke one outright.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed children's residential or day treatment provider operating out of compliance.
channels.how: File through the Department's certification and licensing complaint form. Check the provider directory first: Pennsylvania publishes each facility's licensing status and its completed inspection reports.
channels.note: The Department publishes a quarterly licensing report and an online provider directory carrying every licensed facility's status and inspection history.

civil: The civil SOL for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM claims against all defendants is age 55.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for many CSA offenses and the SOL is age 55 for all other CSA felonies and misdemeanors.
Trafficking: There is no SOL for trafficking offenses.
CSAM: The SOL is age 55 for CSAM offenses.

states.note: Rhode Island's reporting law names this industry directly: under RIGL 40-11-3 every person in the state must report suspected child abuse or neglect within 24 hours, and the law defines abuse to include injury, sexual abuse or exploitation, negligent treatment or maltreatment by any employee of a residential facility or any staff person providing out-of-home care. The same department licenses those facilities and takes the reports.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Three years for injuries to the person, which covers assault, battery and negligence.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the three years start at 18, so the deadline is your 21st birthday.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Tort claims against the state, a city or town must be filed within three years of the injury; for a city or town, the claim must first be presented to the town or city council.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Three years. Rhode Island's felony child abuse law (Brendan's Law) has no special deadline, so the general three-year rule applies, with no pause until the child turns 18.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Three years for felony assault, and three years for misdemeanor assault as well.

channels.name: Rhode Island Department of Health, licensee complaints
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and disciplines Rhode Island's clinical mental health counselors, marriage and family therapists, social workers and psychologists through its boards, and takes complaints against all of them through one route.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed mental health professional in Rhode Island.
channels.how: Submit a complaint through the Department's licensee complaints page.
channels.phone_note: Psychology Licensing Board. Department main line 401-222-5500.

channels.name: Rhode Island DCYF Licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Under RI General Law 42-72.1 the Department of Children, Youth and Families licenses, monitors and enforces the regulations for every foster home, residential facility and child-placing agency in the state.
channels.who_to_report: A Rhode Island residential facility.
channels.how: Complain to the Department's licensing staff. If you are not satisfied with the decision, there is a right of appeal to a judicial forum.

channels.name: Rhode Island Child Abuse Hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line, open around the clock. Rhode Island law defines reportable abuse to include maltreatment by any employee of a residential facility or staff person providing out-of-home care, so conduct inside a program is squarely covered.
channels.who_to_report: A child under 18 at a Rhode Island program. Every person in Rhode Island is required to report within 24 hours of knowing or suspecting.
channels.how: Call. All calls are recorded, and you may call anonymously.
channels.phone_note: 1-800-RI-CHILD. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
channels.deadline: The duty is to report within 24 hours of knowing or suspecting - a deadline on the reporter, not on the abuse.

channels.name: Disability Rights Rhode Island
channels.what_it_can_do: Rhode Island's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A Rhode Island program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for all CSA claims against all defendants is age 53 with a 7-year discovery rule and revival up to age 53 against perpetrators only.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for trafficking claims against perpetrators is age 28.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM claims against all defendants is age 53.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for certain CSA felonies. For any remaining felonies and misdemeanors, the SOL is 3 years from the offense.
Trafficking: The SOL for trafficking is 10 years from the offense.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM violations is 3 years from the offense.

states.note: South Carolina has a division specifically for this: Out of Home Abuse and Neglect, inside the Department of Social Services, which handles abuse and neglect of people in facilities rather than in family homes. That is the right first call for something that happened inside a program, and it has its own daytime and after-hours numbers.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Three years for assault, battery or injury from negligence, counted from when you knew or should have known you had a claim. False imprisonment has a shorter two-year deadline.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Time spent under 18 does not count, but the extra time can never go past one year after your 18th birthday. So a person hurt as a child has at least until age 19, or longer if the normal three years from the injury (or from discovery) ends later.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Claims against the state or a county, city or other local government under the Tort Claims Act must be filed in court within two years of when the loss was or should have been discovered, or within three years if a verified claim was first filed with the agency (that claim is due within one year). Being a minor extends this under the rule above.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: No time limit. South Carolina has no general statute of limitations for crimes, so child abuse can be charged at any time.
items.citation: No statute; South Carolina has no general criminal statute of limitations

items.label: Assault
items.summary: No time limit for felony or misdemeanor assault. South Carolina has no general statute of limitations for crimes.
items.citation: No statute; South Carolina has no general criminal statute of limitations

channels.name: South Carolina Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, Office of Investigations and Enforcement
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates complaints against licensed professionals - including professional counselors, marriage and family therapists, psychologists and social workers - and against unlicensed people practising a profession that requires a licence, to decide whether the facts alleged could breach the law regulating that profession.
channels.who_to_report: Any licensed mental health professional in South Carolina, or somebody practising without the licence.
channels.how: Use the online complaint system, or call. State the facts briefly and clearly, give the name, address and phone number of every witness and what each of them knows, and attach any documents, records, statements or contracts that help.
channels.phone_note: Complaints. The Counselors board direct line is 803-896-4658.
channels.mail: SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, 110 Centerview Dr, Columbia, SC 29210
channels.note: The Department puts the burden on you: it says the complaining party is responsible for making sure everything needed is on the form.

channels.name: South Carolina DSS, Out of Home Abuse and Neglect (OHAN)
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Social Services division that investigates abuse and neglect of people living in facilities, as distinct from abuse in a family home.
channels.who_to_report: A young person abused or neglected inside a South Carolina facility. This is the right first call for something that happened in a program.
channels.how: Call the daytime line during office hours, or the after-hours number outside them.

channels.name: South Carolina child abuse and neglect hotline
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Social Services 24-hour line for reporting suspected child abuse or neglect.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a South Carolina program. For abuse inside a facility, Out of Home Abuse and Neglect is the more specific route.
channels.how: Call.
channels.phone_note: 1-888-CARE4US. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights South Carolina
channels.what_it_can_do: South Carolina's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. It publishes its own guide to reporting abuse in a facility, naming each agency.
channels.who_to_report: A South Carolina program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line, or start from its reporting guide.

channels.name: South Carolina DSS child care and residential licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: Sets the licensing standards for child care and group care facilities in South Carolina, inspects against them, investigates complaints and takes enforcement action. On receiving a regulatory complaint it must carry out an unannounced inspection of the facility.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed facility, where the problem is a regulatory breach rather than a specific allegation of abuse.
channels.how: File through the Department's complaint route. A complaint alleging immediate danger to children is investigated within 24 to 48 hours.
channels.note: The unannounced inspection is the point: a regulatory complaint forces the state through the door without warning.

civil: The civil SOL for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM claims against all defendants is age 27 with a discovery rule.
criminal: There is no criminal SOL for any felonies or misdemeanors, including for CSA, trafficking, and CSAM.

states.note: South Dakota's child protection intake runs on office hours only - 8am to 5pm Central on weekdays - and the state tells you to call local law enforcement instead for anything urgent outside them. Its counseling board is unusually frank that the process is slow: the licensee gets 20 days to answer, everything then goes to a board member, and the Board says the whole thing is generally lengthy.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: Two years for assault, battery or false imprisonment. Three years for other personal injury claims, such as negligence.

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: Time spent under 18 does not count, but the extra time can never go past one year after your 18th birthday. So a person hurt as a child has at least until age 19, or longer if the normal period from the injury ends later.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: For injury claims against the state, a county, city, school district or other public entity, written notice must be given within 180 days of the injury. The notice does not extend the lawsuit deadline.

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Abuse of or cruelty to a minor (a felony) can be charged at any time before the victim turns 25. If the abuse is charged as aggravated assault instead, the limit is seven years from the offense.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Seven years for aggravated assault and other lower-level felonies. Misdemeanor simple assault also has seven years.

channels.name: South Dakota Board of Examiners for Counselors and Marriage and Family Therapists
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses counselors and marriage and family therapists in South Dakota and reviews complaints against them, with board members investigating where needed.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor or marriage and family therapist in South Dakota. Social workers and psychologists have their own boards, which share an office in Spearfish on 605-642-1600.
channels.how: Complete the Board's complaint form. A copy goes to the licensee, who has 20 days to respond in writing; everything then goes to a board member for review and any investigation.
channels.mail: SD Board of Examiners for Counselors and Marriage and Family Therapists, P.O. Box 340, 1351 N. Harrison Ave., Pierre, SD 57501-0340
channels.note: All complaint proceedings are held in executive session, and the Board warns the process is generally lengthy.

channels.name: South Dakota Child Protection Services
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line for child abuse and neglect, run by the Department of Social Services.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a South Dakota program.
channels.how: Call during office hours. For an emergency before 8am, after 5pm, at a weekend or on a holiday, the Department tells you to contact local law enforcement instead.
channels.phone_note: Intake specialists 8am to 5pm Central, Monday to Friday. Outside those hours, call local law enforcement.

channels.name: South Dakota DSS licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Social Services licenses South Dakota's foster homes and residential facilities and maintains the state's abuse registry, which bars people from working in these settings.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed South Dakota facility.
channels.how: Contact the Department. Abuse and neglect go to Child Protection Services.
channels.phone_note: Child Protection Services intake also takes concerns about licensed facilities.

channels.name: Disability Rights South Dakota
channels.what_it_can_do: South Dakota's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy.
channels.who_to_report: A South Dakota program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line.

civil: CSA: The civil SOL for CSA claims against all defendants is age 19 with a 3-year discovery rule that has an upper age limit of 40 years for claims against non-perpetrator defendants.
Trafficking: The civil SOL for trafficking claims is age 24.
CSAM: The civil SOL for CSAM claims is age 24.
criminal: CSA: There is no criminal SOL for first- and second-degree rape. The SOL is either age 25 or 7 years from the offense for other felonies and misdemeanors.
Trafficking: The SOL is 7 years from the offense for trafficking.
CSAM: The SOL for CSAM is 7 years from the offense.

states.note: Three Tennessee specifics. The abuse hotline stops taking calls at weekends - from 11pm Central Friday to 11pm Central Sunday it plays a recording sending you to the online portal - so if something happens on a Saturday, use the portal. Licensing splits on whether a program calls itself clinical: DCS licenses the non-clinical residential programs, the Health Facilities Commission licenses the healthcare facilities. And unlike most states, the Department of Health says it will not reveal a complainant's name to the practitioner.

items.label: Physical abuse or injury
items.summary: One year for personal injury, including assault, battery, negligence and false imprisonment. It becomes two years if the person who hurt you is criminally prosecuted for it (and you sue that person).

items.label: If it happened before you turned 18
items.summary: If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the clock starts at 18. With the one-year injury deadline, that means suing before your 19th birthday.

items.label: If the program was run by or for the government
items.summary: Claims against a county, city or other local government must be filed within 12 months. Claims against the State go to the Claims Commission: written notice must be given to the state's Division of Claims and Risk Management within the normal deadline for that kind of claim (one year for injury).

items.label: Physical child abuse
items.summary: Aggravated child abuse, neglect or endangerment (serious injury, a weapon, or torture): until 10 years after the victim turns 18, or longer if the normal felony period is longer. Ordinary felony child abuse of a teenager (injury, Class E felony): only two years from the offense.

items.label: Assault
items.summary: Four years for most aggravated assault (Class C or D felony). Misdemeanor assault must be charged within 12 months.

channels.name: Tennessee Department of Health, Health Related Boards, Office of Investigations
channels.what_it_can_do: Investigates complaints against every mental health practitioner the state licenses - professional counselors, marital and family therapists, clinical pastoral therapists, social workers and psychologists - through one Office of Investigations. A board consultant and a department attorney decide whether the statutes or rules were broken.
channels.what_it_cannot_do: If they conclude there was no statutory violation the file is closed, and all you get is a letter telling you so.
channels.who_to_report: Any licensed or certified mental health practitioner in Tennessee.
channels.how: Complete an Allegations Report form and the voluntary Release of Information form, attach your evidence, and send them in. Call the Office of Investigations first if you want to talk it through, or to ask whether the practitioner has been disciplined before.
channels.phone_note: Office of Investigations. Board office 615-741-5735, or 1-800-778-4123 nationwide.
channels.mail: Health Related Boards, 665 Mainstream Drive, 2nd Floor, Nashville, TN 37243
channels.note: Your name is not revealed to the practitioner - the Department says the complainant's identity is confidential. You are given a complaint number and written notice when the case reaches a disposition. A complaint only becomes public if the Department files a notice of charges. The Department's website was being relaunched when this was checked, so some of its pages have moved.

channels.name: Tennessee Health Facilities Commission, Complaint Intake Unit
channels.what_it_can_do: Licenses and regulates healthcare facilities in Tennessee and takes complaints against licensed, certified and unlicensed ones alike - the unlicensed part matters in this industry. It publishes facility action and abuse reports, and survey deficiencies for any facility taking Medicare or TennCare.
channels.who_to_report: A facility providing clinical treatment, or one you believe is operating without a licence.
channels.how: Use the public complaints portal, call the intake unit, or ask them to post you a complaint form.
